A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work, and their text, equations, tables and figures are readable. Neither supplied PDF contains appendices. v2 refers to separate supplemental results that are unavailable; no conclusions about their contents are inferred.

before.justification: v1 reports original experiments on four text-to-video models, including attack success rates, semantic similarity, qualitative examples and ablations.

after.justification: v2 reports original experimental results for the revised method on the same four models, including numerical comparisons and ablations.

M1.justification: v2 adds an unsafe-frame occupancy objective, weighted by gamma, to the previous filter-bypass and semantic-consistency objectives. Its displayed semantic loss also omits v1's (1-F) gate on video-caption consistency, and its stopping rule permits convergence. These change the specified optimization procedure; the underlying language-model optimizer and prompt mutation remain.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate 700 prompts sampled from the same 14 T2VSafetyBench categories on Pika, Luma, Kling and Open-Sora. No additional dataset, domain or distinct test scenario is reported.

E2.justification: Table 2 in both versions evaluates the same two baselines, T2VSafetyBench and DACA, against the proposed method on all four models. Newly cited methods are not added to the experimental comparisons.

E3.justification: Reported defaults change from lambda=1 and beta=1 to lambda=3 and beta=2, with gamma=1 added. The lambda and beta sensitivity ranges also change. Model versions, sample counts, evaluation metrics, the 20-iteration budget and five variants remain unchanged. These are reported setting revisions, not independent evidence that experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: Both versions retain lambda, beta, iteration-count and prompt-mutation ablations, with revised settings and outcomes. v1's variant-count sensitivity study, Figure 7 and Section 4.4.4, is absent from the supplied v2. v2 announces a gamma ablation but presents no corresponding results; its unavailable supplement cannot establish an added analysis.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental seed counts, repeated-run uncertainty, confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests. Averaging prompt-variant scores is an optimization operation, not statistical uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: The proposed method's numerical evidence is revised throughout Tables 1-3 and the retained sensitivity plots. For example, Open-Sora GPT-4/human ASR changes from 64.4%/66.3% to 67.1%/68.7%, while similarity changes from 0.272 to 0.269; Pika changes from 53.6%/55.0% to 55.9%/57.6%, with similarity falling from 0.268 to 0.266. Baseline scores and overall rankings remain unchanged. These are replacement results under a revised objective and weights, not isolated same-setting gains.

T1.justification: Beyond v1's similarity and filter definitions, v2 introduces a formal frame-token attention relation, an attention-concentration premise, a thresholded unsafe-frame ratio and the associated loss formulation. It also adds a mathematical mutation-selection rule. These substantively extend the mathematical specification without adding proofs. As written, the selection rule averages over the same fixed candidate set, so its objective does not distinguish the candidate being selected.

C1.justification: The central claim of a first optimization-based T2V jailbreak framework with semantic preservation and mutation is retained. v2 narrows the novelty wording toward discrete optimization and extends the claimed objective to sustained unsafe-frame generation. Quantitative headlines also change: v1's 39-point Pika advantage corresponds to GPT-4 evaluation against DACA, whereas v2's 7-point headline corresponds to human evaluation against T2VSafetyBench.

C2.justification: v2 adds a temporal-attention explanation for unsafe frames and hypotheses attributing model differences to moderation strategies. Its conclusion explicitly identifies video-feedback query costs as a limitation and proposes local proxies or query optimization as future remedies. v1's interpretation that GPT-4/human agreement validates automated evaluation is omitted.

D1.justification: v2 removes v1's exact initialization, paraphrasing and mutation instructions, the specified SneakyPrompt unsafe-word-list source, and the description of score normalization to 0-100. It also replaces the explicit one-frame-per-second output-filter sampling instruction with unspecified frame sampling. Revised loss weights are supplied, but the new frame-similarity threshold delta is not specified. These substantially reduce procedural detail without establishing that the omitted practices actually changed.

R1.justification: v2 adds contextual references including Inception, T2VShield and additional video-generation and adversarial-learning works, while removing several earlier background references. Section 2.3 more explicitly contrasts discrete optimization and agent-guided mutation with static prompts and manual replacement. The central positioning relative to T2VSafetyBench and existing T2I jailbreak approaches remains.

P1.justification: The paper is renamed T2V-OptJail, and the abstract, introduction, related work, method exposition and conclusion are extensively rewritten. The method is reorganized around filter bypassing, semantic consistency and mutation; setup and ablation subsections are consolidated. This is substantial narrative restructuring beyond the scientific additions.

P2.justification: v2 changes the document from two columns to one and completely redraws Figure 1. Tables 2 and 3 become stacked model blocks, the same two qualitative examples are merged into Figure 2, and three retained sensitivity studies are combined into dual-axis panels in Figure 3. The variant-count plot is no longer displayed.

improvement.justification: v2 provides clearer organization, more readable comparison tables and an explicit query-cost limitation. However, it removes concrete optimizer instructions and sampling details supplied in v1, leaves the new frame-occupancy threshold unspecified, and introduces a selection equation that does not distinguish candidates. The supplied results also do not isolate the new frame-occupancy component. These losses in reproducibility and mathematical precision outweigh the presentation gains; higher ASR under changed objectives and settings does not resolve them.
